body: Earbuds in at the stop, and whatever was queued from yesterday starts itself: twelve minutes past six, the second bus, the one that is never full, a man with his forehead against the window because the glass is cold and he has not properly woken up. Nine minutes later it hands him to something else, and that to a bulletin, and by the time the bus reaches the dual carriageway he is quietly furious about a decision taken in a country he will never visit. He gets off at the depot carrying it, and he will still be carrying it at eleven.

Nobody did that to him, which is the part worth sitting with. No employer required it, no family asked for it, there was no meeting about it. It filled the one part of his day nothing else had a claim on, because he never made a claim on it either.

Look honestly at a working day and count the hours that are actually yours. Not free — yours, in the sense that you decide what occupies your attention. For most people the answer sits near zero, with a single exception, and it is the one nobody thinks of as time off.

It is worth being exact about why the commute is different, because the reason is odd. It is simultaneously obligatory and unsupervised. You have to be there — the bus goes where it goes and the traffic does what it does — and while you are there, nobody can require anything of you. No colleague can reach you. No child needs anything. There is nothing you could be doing instead that you are failing to do, which is the rarest condition in an adult life. Everything else in a day is either owed to somebody or borrowed from something. This one is neither.
The dial this article ends at runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 stations, of which 46 are on air. Every one is playing right now, on a schedule set before you got in the car.

That last detail is the expensive one, and it is deliberate. A station already running cannot be tailored to you, cannot wait to learn your taste, and cannot ask you a question at half past six when you are in no condition to answer one. Somebody decided hours ago and left it going. It costs far more to programme a day properly than to hand a listener a search box and call it choice. Everybody wants that hour. Most days it is the only one where you get to decide what goes in — and deciding, properly understood, can mean deciding once, in advance, rather than forty times at a junction.

It should be obvious how much competes for the slot. Every news service, podcast network and streaming platform is designed around this hour, because it is the only one left where a person is reliably alone with a pair of speakers. Most of what fills it leaves people arriving in a slightly worse condition than they set out in: better informed, more agitated, no readier for the room they are about to walk into. That is not wickedness on anybody’s part. It is what gets built when the thing being measured is how long you stayed, and nobody measures what state you were in getting out of the car.

The dial is arranged so that you can learn where things live and stop deciding. There is a five-fold band of ministry stations, a multilanguage band for the nations and a mainstream band of always-on formats, and the frequencies do not move. Learn roughly where a thing sits and your hand goes to it without your attention going with it, which matters more at ten past six than at any other hour. Anyone who grew up with a car radio can still find a station in the dark.
So the question is not what you want to listen to. At that hour, nobody knows what they want.

The obvious answer is a playlist you made yourself, and it deserves a fair hearing, because a good one is a genuinely good thing and there is nothing wrong with knowing what you like. The trouble is what it cannot do. A playlist only ever returns songs you already knew to put on it, which means the drive home from a bad day is scored by a person who was in a different mood when they built it. And it still asks. Every morning it opens with a question, answered by whichever version of you is holding the phone at six — the tired one, the one with the meeting at nine, the one who picks whatever requires nothing. Choice at that hour is not freedom. It is one more small task.
A dial plays whether or not you chose.

A woman finishes a night on a hospital ward at twenty past seven and drives home with the window down because the air keeps her awake. She does not want to talk to anybody. She has had the same station on for a year and could not tell you what plays most mornings. Four minutes from the house a set of lights always catches her, and she sits at them with the engine running while a choir comes in behind an organ, the way they do when a song has already been going a while. She has stopped gripping the wheel. When she pulls onto the drive her son is at the window and she has enough left to be pleased about it, which she did not have when the shift ended.
Nothing there was chosen and nothing there was arranged. She got four minutes at a red light of something that was not asking her for anything, and it turned out that four minutes was the difference.

There is a cost to this and it needs stating without hedging. A station will play you a song you would not have picked, at exactly the moment you are stuck behind a lorry and already late. It will play a style you find corny, and run a programme you would have skipped past in a list, and there is no skip, because you are not the editor. Some mornings the honest answer is that silence would have served you better, and a broadcast cannot know that about you.

The irritation is not a fault in the format; it is the format. The whole value of handing an hour to somebody else is that they will not give you back exactly what you already had. Nobody was ever changed by the playlist they built themselves — it is a mirror with a play button. The song that arrives when you wanted nothing is the only kind that can get past the version of you holding the phone at six.

So the argument is narrow and practical. The commute is the last uncontested slot in most lives. It will be filled by something, and that something gets chosen either once, deliberately, by you, or forty times a week by whatever happens to autoplay. Handing it to a frequency is not giving the hour away. It is the only version of the hour where you decided what goes in and then got to stop deciding.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

The band carries four kinds of programming and it is worth knowing they are there before you start turning. There is music, which is most of it — praise and worship, contemporary, country, gospel, hymns and a good deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained rather than sung. There is family programming, safe to have on with children in the back. And there are the international stations, hosted in their own languages rather than translated into them afterwards — 40 of them across 29 languages. Four kinds, one dial, and nothing that asks you a question at a set of traffic lights.

For a commute, start at HM 302.50 — Pentecostal Shout. It is the one this argument actually points at, for a reason that has nothing to do with genre preference. The commute is the only hour in a working week where nobody can see you, and a car is therefore the last place most adults can sing at full volume without being observed doing it. Energetic gospel is the format that asks you to, and it is wasted in an open-plan office and awkward in a kitchen with other people in it. Imani Inspire hosts it, the Gospel Fire Hour runs in the evening for the journey back, and it is there on both sides of the working day whether you are in the car or not. It will not sit politely in the background, which is exactly why it belongs in the one hour that is asking nothing of you.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone is in your pocket, press play, and it plays — it is deliberately built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. Add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else on it. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It is free, it keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band finds out which frequencies people reach for at six in the morning — which is how the next one gets programmed.

So treat this as an invitation rather than an offer. Do not audition it and do not evaluate it on the way to work — those are desk words and this is a car. Put HM 302.50 on tomorrow before you pull out, and then leave it alone for the whole journey. Give it a fortnight of ordinary mornings and you will know whether that hour is better spent this way, without having made a single decision at a junction to find out.
